summary: Describes a standard method for storing Diffie-Hellman keys in the DNS using KEY resource records. It was later updated by RFC 6944.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2539 defines a way to store Diffie-Hellman public keys in the DNS, using the KEY record with algorithm number 2. A record holds the large prime, the generator and the party's public value, and two well-known groups are defined so that a common prime and generator need not be sent over the network.

subtitle: How to publish Diffie-Hellman public keys in DNS KEY records, with a table of well-known prime and generator pairs.

tldr.problem: Two parties that want a shared secret can use Diffie-Hellman, but they need the same prime and generator and a way to publish their own public values. The DNS had no record type that could carry this.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a KEY resource record with algorithm number 2 that holds the prime, the generator and the public value, and adds a table of well-known prime and generator pairs so that the prime can be named by index instead of sent in full.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2539 is a Proposed Standard from March 1999 and has been updated by RFC 6944.

facts.label: Prime and generator pairs in the table

today: RFC 2539 is a Proposed Standard from March 1999 and has been updated by RFC 6944. The KEY record with algorithm number 2 remains the way this specification stores Diffie-Hellman public keys in the DNS.

sections.title: Why Store Diffie-Hellman Keys in the DNS
sections.content:
The DNS is the global hierarchical, replicated and distributed database used for Internet addressing, mail proxy and similar information. It has already been extended to carry digital signatures and cryptographic keys, as described in RFC 2535, so it can be used to distribute keys securely.

This document describes how to store Diffie-Hellman keys in the DNS, and assumes familiarity with the Diffie-Hellman key exchange algorithm. It adds a record type and format on top of the existing KEY record, rather than a new record type of its own.
sections.plainLanguage: The DNS already carries signed keys, so it can be used to publish the public halves of a Diffie-Hellman exchange. This RFC says which values go into a KEY record and how they are laid out.

sections.title: How the Diffie-Hellman Exchange Works
sections.content:
Diffie-Hellman needs two parties to interact so that both end up with the same keying material, which can then be used for authentication. The RFC works through the arithmetic. Two parties hold local secrets i and j and each calculates a public value: X is g to the power i, modulo p, and Y is g to the power j, modulo p. They exchange those two values, and each then calculates a shared value: Zi is Y to the power i, modulo p, and Zj is X to the power j, modulo p.

Both parties arrive at the same shared secret, which an adversary who does not know i or j cannot learn from the exchanged messages. That holds unless the adversary can recover i or j by performing a discrete logarithm modulo p, which is hard when p and g are strong.

The private key of each party is its secret i or j. The public key is the pair p and g, which must be the same for both parties, together with that party's own X or Y.

The RFC also explains why there is no separate Diffie-Hellman SIG record. DNS SIG records are mainly used as stored authenticators of zone information for many different resolvers, and no Diffie-Hellman SIG record is defined.
sections.plainLanguage: Each side keeps a secret number, sends out a value computed from it, and both sides turn the two exchanged values into the same shared secret. The private part is the secret number; the public part is the prime, the generator and the value sent out.

sections.title: The KEY Resource Record
sections.content:
Diffie-Hellman keys are stored as KEY resource records with algorithm number 2. The first four octets of the record data are the flags, protocol and algorithm fields common to all KEY records. The rest, from the prime length through the public value, is the public key part of the record.

The prime length field holds the length of the prime p in bytes when that length is 16 or greater. The prime field holds the binary form of the prime, most significant byte first. If the prime length field is 1 or 2, then the prime field is not a prime at all: it is an unsigned index into a table of 65,536 prime and generator pairs, and the generator length should then be zero. A value of zero, or 3 through 15, in the prime length field is reserved.

The generator length field holds the length of the generator g in bytes, and the generator field holds the binary form of the generator, most significant byte first. The public value length field holds the length of the public value, which is g to the power i, modulo p, in bytes, and the public value field holds that value in binary, most significant byte first.

The period of key validity is not part of the KEY record. It is given by the SIG record or records that sign and authenticate the KEY records at that domain name. No format is defined for an algorithm 2 SIG record, because that record is not used.
sections.plainLanguage: The record holds the prime, the generator and the party's public value, each with its own length field. When the prime length is 1 or 2, the prime field is really an index into a table of standard prime and generator pairs.

sections.title: Performance Considerations
sections.content:
DNS implementations are optimised for small transfers, typically less than 512 bytes including overhead. Larger transfers do work correctly, and work is under way to make them more efficient, but it is still advisable to keep the size of the KEY record sets stored in the DNS as small as is consistent with adequate security.

The RFC adds a further point: in a secure zone, an authenticating SIG record is returned as well, so the size of the answer is larger than the KEY records alone.
sections.plainLanguage: DNS is built for small answers, so the RFC asks that the number and size of stored key records be kept as small as security allows. In a signed zone, the signature records add to the answer as well.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
Giving a meaning to the prime length values of 0 and 3 through 15 requires IETF consensus.

The allocation of the table of prime and generator pairs is split into three ranges. The well-known pairs numbered 0x0000 through 0x07FF can only be assigned by an IETF standards action, and this Proposed Standard assigns 0x0001 through 0x0002. The pairs numbered 0x0800 through 0xBFFF can be assigned on the basis of RFC documentation. The pairs numbered 0xC000 through 0xFFFF are available for private use and are not centrally coordinated, and using such private pairs outside a closed environment may lead to conflicts.

The appendix lists the two pairs this document assigns. Group 1 is a 768-bit prime with the generator 2, and group 2 is a 1024-bit prime with the generator 2. The appendix gives each prime as a formula, a decimal value and its hexadecimal form, and notes that the numbers were copied from the IPsec effort, where the derivation is explained more fully.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC assigns the first two entries of the table of standard prime and generator pairs, and explains which ranges IANA, an RFC or private use can fill. The two assigned entries are a 768-bit and a 1024-bit prime, both with the generator 2.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Many of the general security considerations from RFC 2535 apply. Keys retrieved from the DNS should not be trusted unless they have been obtained securely from a secure resolver or independently verified by the user, and unless that resolver and that secure obtainment or independent verification conform to security policies the user accepts. As with all cryptographic algorithms, evaluating the necessary strength of the key matters, and that depends on local policy.

The usual Diffie-Hellman key strength considerations apply as well: (p-1)/2 should also be prime, g should be primitive modulo p, and p should be large.
sections.plainLanguage: A key fetched from the DNS is only as trustworthy as the path it came by, so the RFC requires a secure resolver or independent verification. The prime and the generator also have to be strong enough for the purpose.

viz.caption: THE DIFFIE-HELLMAN VALUES AS THE RFC WRITES THEM

data.title: The exchange
data.code:
X = g**i ( mod p )   Y = g**j ( mod p )

Zi = Y**i ( mod p )   Zj = X**j ( mod p )

viz.caption: THE FIELDS OF THE ALGORITHM 2 KEY RECORD

items.label: 4 octets
items.desc: The fields common to all KEY records. The algorithm is 2.

items.label: 16 bits
items.desc: Length of the prime in bytes when it is 16 or greater.

items.label: variable
items.desc: The prime p, most significant byte first, or an index into the table of prime and generator pairs.

items.label: 16 bits
items.desc: Length of the generator g in bytes. Should be zero when the prime field is an index.

items.label: variable
items.desc: The generator g, most significant byte first.

items.label: 16 bits
items.desc: Length of the public value in bytes.

items.label: variable
items.desc: The Diffie-Hellman public value, g**i (mod p), most significant byte first.
